idea: Friendly-fraud customer wakes up a dormant card on a new phone and disputes the large purchase; Assay lacks innocence signals (home_region/tenure disabled) and triggers the dormant wakeup detector (LR 5.65) plus customer_report prior, falsely blocking and reporting a legitimate cardholder.

case.trigger_text: Cardholder called to dispute $1,485.00 online charge (e2) and $19.99 charge (e1). States card has been locked in a home safe for months and was never used.

truth.why_it_should_fool_assay: This is first-party friendly fraud (the customer actually made the purchases from their home billing region and email, then lied to get $1,500 back). Because Assay switched off home_region and long_tenure_clean innocence signals, and treats dormant wakeup (LR 5.65) + new device + customer_report as confirmed third-party fraud, it will output BLOCK_CARD and FILE_REPORT on a legitimate transaction.

idea: Genuine account takeover where the thief spoofs the cardholder's home device profile or uses in-person/no-device channels and drains the card over 96 hours before the victim notices and disputes; Assay's episode builder caps at 1h (and 48h only for a *new* device), severely undercounting the fraud exposure.

case.trigger_text: Customer reports account takeover via compromised desktop session; disputes e5 ($890.00) and all four preceding out-of-region charges (e1-e4) over the past 4 days totaling $2,960.00.

truth.why_it_should_fool_assay: Assay's episode builder (`B34_episode.md`) uses a strict 1-hour window cap, extending to 48 hours only when transactions occur on a *new* device. Because the attacker compromised the customer's existing session (`device: home`) and spaced the 5 charges more than 1 hour apart (and up to 92h before open), Assay will only count e5 ($890) instead of all 5 transactions ($2,960), missing 80% of the transactions and failing to cross the $2,500 L2 routing threshold.

idea: Genuine fraud victim whose card is billed $49.99 three times over 60 hours by a crooked merchant mimicking a recurring subscription, triggering a customer dispute that looks like Policy R7 (disputed recurring charge) while actually being third-party CNP fraud.

case.trigger_text: Customer disputes $49.99 recurring-style subscription charge (e3) and two identical $49.99 charges over the past three days (e1, e2). Customer states they never signed up for this service.

truth.why_it_should_fool_assay: If Assay checks for Policy R7 (Disputed but legitimate recurring pattern: same product/amount/email/home region with low risk_score), it will misclassify this genuine 3-day cramming fraud as a legitimate recurring dispute and refuse to block the card. Conversely, if Assay calls it fraud, its 1h episode cap (with `device: none`) will only count e3 ($49.99) and miss e1 and e2 (67% undercounted).

case.trigger_text: Cardholder A disputes $320.00 online purchase (e4), claiming they did not authorize the transaction after family members used the household tablet for group ticket purchases.

truth.why_it_should_fool_assay: Four cards sharing a new device profile, recipient email, product, and region within a 3-hour window plus a `customer_report` trigger will fire Assay's CPC / charge-shape / ring detectors (LR 8.52 to 68.66), causing Assay to declare high-probability organized fraud (`BLOCK_CARD`, `FILE_REPORT`, `MONITOR_CONNECTED_CARDS`) on what is actually a legitimate household purchase followed by friendly-fraud buyer's remorse.
